easy.text: What force pulls objects toward the ground?

options.text: Gravity
options.feedback: Correct -- gravity pulls objects with mass toward each other, and toward Earth's center.

options.text: Magnetism
options.feedback: Magnetism only affects magnetic materials, not all falling objects.

options.text: Friction
options.feedback: Friction opposes motion between surfaces, it doesn't pull objects downward.

options.text: Air pressure
options.feedback: Air pressure can affect falling objects slightly, but it isn't the main force pulling them down.

medium.text: Ignoring air resistance, how do a heavy ball and a light ball fall when dropped from the same height at the same time?

options.text: They fall at the same rate and land at the same time
options.feedback: Correct -- without air resistance, gravity accelerates all objects at the same rate regardless of mass.

options.text: The heavy ball falls much faster
options.feedback: Without air resistance, mass doesn't affect the rate of free fall.

options.text: The light ball falls much faster
options.feedback: Without air resistance, mass doesn't affect the rate of free fall.

options.text: Neither ball falls at all
options.feedback: Gravity acts on both objects, so both will fall.

hard.text: A feather and a hammer are dropped together in a vacuum chamber with no air. What happens?

options.text: They hit the ground at the same time, since air resistance is eliminated
options.feedback: Correct -- with no air resistance, gravity alone determines fall rate, which is the same for all masses.

options.text: The hammer hits first because it's heavier
options.feedback: This would be true with air resistance, but in a vacuum, mass doesn't affect fall rate.

options.text: The feather hits first because it's lighter
options.feedback: Lighter objects don't fall faster -- without air resistance, both fall at the same rate.

options.text: Neither object falls in a vacuum
options.feedback: Gravity still acts in a vacuum -- only air resistance is removed, not gravity itself.

easy.hard: This force acts between any two masses, pulling them toward each other.
easy.medium: This is the invisible pull that brings falling objects back down to Earth.
easy.easy: This is the force that makes things fall down instead of floating away.

medium.hard: In the absence of air resistance, the acceleration due to gravity is the same for every object, regardless of how much mass it has.
medium.medium: Without air slowing things down, gravity speeds up every object equally, no matter its weight.
medium.easy: Without air slowing them down, heavy and light objects actually fall at the same speed.

hard.hard: This scenario removes the one variable (air resistance) that normally makes lighter, less aerodynamic objects fall slower -- without it, gravity's acceleration is identical for all masses.
hard.medium: Removing air resistance means the only remaining force is gravity, which affects every object the same way regardless of weight.
hard.easy: With no air to slow the feather down, both objects fall at exactly the same rate.

easy.text: What is the main purpose of a pulley?

options.text: To change the direction of a force, making it easier to lift objects
options.feedback: Correct -- a pulley lets you pull down to lift something up, and can reduce the effort needed.

options.text: To generate electricity
options.feedback: Generating electricity is not the function of a basic pulley system.

options.text: To measure the weight of an object
options.feedback: A pulley helps move objects, it isn't a weight-measuring tool like a scale.

options.text: To convert heat into motion
options.feedback: A pulley works through mechanical force, not heat conversion.

medium.text: How does a system of multiple pulleys generally affect the effort force needed to lift a load?

options.text: It reduces the effort force needed, though you must pull a longer distance
options.feedback: Correct -- more pulleys distribute the load's weight across multiple rope segments, reducing effort at the cost of pulling further.

options.text: It always requires more effort force than lifting directly
options.feedback: The whole benefit of adding pulleys is typically to reduce the effort force required, not increase it.

options.text: It has no effect on the effort force at all
options.feedback: Adding pulleys does change the mechanical advantage, directly affecting the effort needed.

options.text: It eliminates the need for any force entirely
options.feedback: Some force is still needed -- pulleys reduce the required effort, they don't eliminate it.

hard.text: A pulley system has a mechanical advantage of 4. If a load weighs 200 N, approximately how much effort force is needed to lift it (ignoring friction)?

options.feedback: Correct -- effort = load ÷ mechanical advantage = 200÷4 = 50.
This multiplies instead of dividing the load by the mechanical advantage.
This ignores the mechanical advantage entirely.

options.text: 4 N
options.feedback: This doesn't correctly relate the mechanical advantage to the load weight.

easy.hard: This device redirects the line of applied force, often turning a downward pull into an upward lift.
easy.medium: This lets you pull down on a rope to lift something up instead of lifting it directly.
easy.easy: This lets you pull a rope down to lift something up.

medium.hard: Spreading the load's weight across more rope segments reduces the force needed on any single segment, at the cost of needing to pull more rope through.
medium.medium: More pulleys share the load's weight across more rope sections, making each pull easier but longer.
medium.easy: More pulleys make lifting easier, but you have to pull more rope to do it.

hard.hard: Divide the load's weight by the mechanical advantage to find the reduced effort force required.
hard.medium: Divide the load weight by the mechanical advantage number.
hard.easy: Divide 200 by 4 to find the effort force needed.

easy.text: Static electricity is caused by the buildup of what on an object's surface?

options.text: Electric charge
options.feedback: Correct -- static electricity comes from an imbalance of electric charge, usually from electrons moving between surfaces.

options.text: Water molecules
options.feedback: Water isn't what causes static electricity -- in fact, humidity often reduces static buildup.

options.text: Heat energy
options.feedback: Static electricity results from charge imbalance, not from heat.

options.text: Sound waves
options.feedback: Sound waves are unrelated to the buildup of static electric charge.

medium.text: When you rub a balloon on your hair, electrons transfer from your hair to the balloon. What happens next?

options.text: The balloon becomes negatively charged and can stick to a wall
options.feedback: Correct -- gaining extra electrons gives the balloon a negative charge, which can attract it to neutral surfaces.

options.text: The balloon becomes positively charged
options.feedback: Gaining electrons makes the balloon negatively charged, not positively.

options.text: Nothing happens, since electrons don't affect charge
options.feedback: Electron transfer is exactly what creates a charge imbalance and static effects.

options.text: The hair becomes negatively charged instead
options.feedback: Since the hair lost electrons, it becomes positively charged, not negatively.

hard.text: Why does a charged balloon eventually stop sticking to a wall over time?

options.text: The excess charge gradually leaks away into the air or surroundings
options.feedback: Correct -- static charge dissipates over time as it slowly transfers to the surrounding air or other objects.

options.text: The wall becomes magnetic and repels the balloon
options.feedback: Walls don't become magnetic in this scenario -- this is an electric charge phenomenon, not magnetism.

options.text: The balloon's mass increases over time
options.feedback: The balloon's mass doesn't change -- what changes is its electric charge, which slowly dissipates.

options.text: Gravity becomes stronger after a few minutes
options.feedback: Gravity's strength doesn't change over such short time periods -- charge simply leaks away.

easy.hard: This phenomenon results from an imbalance between positive and negative particles on a surface.
easy.medium: This happens when negatively charged particles build up unevenly on a surface.
easy.easy: This is caused by an uneven amount of electric charge building up somewhere.

medium.hard: Whichever object gains extra negatively charged particles ends up with a negative overall charge.
medium.medium: The object that gains extra electrons ends up with a negative charge.
medium.easy: The balloon gained electrons, so figure out what charge that gives it.

hard.hard: Static charge isn't permanent -- it gradually neutralizes as excess electrons find a path to redistribute into the environment.
hard.medium: Over time, the extra charge slowly moves off the balloon and into the air around it.
hard.easy: The extra charge slowly drains away into the air over time.

easy.text: Which of the following is a type of electromagnetic wave?

options.text: X-rays
options.feedback: Correct -- X-rays are a form of electromagnetic radiation used in medical imaging.

options.text: Sound waves
options.feedback: Sound waves are mechanical waves that need a medium, unlike electromagnetic waves.

options.text: Ocean waves
options.feedback: Ocean waves are physical waves in water, not electromagnetic radiation.

options.text: Seismic waves
options.feedback: Seismic waves travel through the earth during events like earthquakes, and are not electromagnetic.

medium.text: Which of the following correctly orders these electromagnetic waves from lowest to highest energy?

options.text: Radio waves, visible light, gamma rays
options.feedback: Correct -- radio waves have the lowest energy/frequency, and gamma rays have the highest, with visible light in between.

options.text: Gamma rays, visible light, radio waves
options.feedback: This lists them from highest to lowest energy, the reverse of what was asked.

options.text: Visible light, radio waves, gamma rays
options.feedback: Radio waves actually have lower energy than visible light, not higher.

options.text: Gamma rays, radio waves, visible light
options.feedback: This doesn't follow a consistent increasing or decreasing energy order.

hard.text: Why are gamma rays more dangerous to living tissue than radio waves?

options.text: Gamma rays carry much more energy per photon, which can damage cells and DNA
options.feedback: Correct -- higher-frequency electromagnetic waves carry more energy, making high-energy radiation like gamma rays capable of causing biological damage.

options.text: Gamma rays travel slower than radio waves
options.feedback: All electromagnetic waves, including gamma rays and radio waves, travel at the same speed (the speed of light) in a vacuum.

options.text: Gamma rays are heavier than radio waves
options.feedback: Electromagnetic waves don't have mass in this sense -- their danger relates to energy, not weight.

options.text: Gamma rays are a completely different kind of wave, unrelated to radio waves
options.feedback: Both are part of the same electromagnetic spectrum -- they differ in energy/frequency, not in fundamental type.

easy.hard: This wave type has a very short wavelength and is used to see through soft tissue in medical settings.
easy.medium: This type of wave can pass through skin, letting doctors see bones in medical images.
easy.easy: This is the type of wave used in medical imaging to see bones.

medium.hard: Arrange the waves by increasing frequency, which corresponds directly to increasing energy.
medium.medium: Order them from the lowest-frequency, lowest-energy wave to the highest.
medium.easy: Start with the wave used for radio broadcasts, end with the highest-energy wave type.

hard.hard: Energy per photon increases with frequency across the electromagnetic spectrum, and gamma rays sit at the highest-frequency, highest-energy end, capable of ionizing and damaging molecules.
hard.medium: Gamma rays carry a lot more energy in each individual wave packet, which is what makes them harmful to cells.
hard.easy: Gamma rays simply carry a lot more energy than radio waves, which is what makes them harmful.

easy.text: In physics, what is the formula for work?

options.text: Work = Force × Distance
options.feedback: Correct -- work is done when a force moves an object over a distance.

options.text: Work = Force + Distance
options.feedback: Work is calculated by multiplying, not adding, force and distance.

options.text: Work = Force ÷ Distance
options.feedback: This isn't the correct relationship -- work involves multiplying force and distance.

options.text: Work = Mass × Distance
options.feedback: Work depends on force, not directly on mass alone.

medium.text: How much work is done when a force of 10 N moves an object 5 meters?

options.text: 50 joules
options.feedback: Correct -- 10 × 5 = 50 joules of work.

options.text: 15 joules
options.feedback: This adds the values instead of multiplying them.

options.text: 2 joules
options.feedback: This divides instead of multiplying the force and distance.

options.text: 10 joules
options.feedback: This ignores the distance factor entirely.

hard.text: A person pushes hard against a heavy wall, but the wall doesn't move at all. According to the physics definition of work, how much work was done on the wall?

options.text: Zero, because there was no displacement
options.feedback: Correct -- since the wall didn't move at all, no work was done on it, regardless of how much force or effort was applied.

options.text: A large amount, since a lot of force and effort was used
options.feedback: Physical effort alone doesn't count as work in this formal sense -- displacement is required.

options.text: A small but nonzero amount, proportional to how tired the person got
options.feedback: Fatigue isn't part of the physics definition of work -- only force and actual displacement matter.

options.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the wall's mass
options.feedback: The wall's mass isn't needed here -- since there's no movement, work is simply zero regardless of mass.

easy.hard: This quantity combines how hard you push with how far the object actually moves.
easy.medium: Multiply the amount of force by how far the object moves.
easy.easy: Multiply force by distance to get work.

medium.hard: Multiply the force value by the distance value to compute the work done.
medium.medium: Multiply 10 by 5 to find the work.
medium.easy: Multiply the force and the distance together.

hard.hard: The physics definition of work requires actual displacement of the object -- effort or force alone, without any resulting movement, produces zero work by definition.
hard.medium: If the object doesn't move any distance at all, no work is done, no matter how much force was applied.
hard.easy: Since the wall doesn't move at all, the distance is zero, so the work done is also zero.

easy.text: What shape is a convex lens?

options.text: Thicker in the middle than at the edges
options.feedback: Correct -- a convex lens bulges outward, thicker in the center.

options.text: Thicker at the edges than in the middle
options.feedback: This describes a concave lens, the opposite shape.

options.text: Perfectly flat all the way across
options.feedback: A flat piece of glass isn't classified as either a convex or concave lens.

options.text: Shaped like a perfect cube
options.feedback: Lenses are curved, not cube-shaped.

medium.text: What does a convex lens typically do to light rays passing through it?

options.text: Converges (focuses) the light rays toward a point
options.feedback: Correct -- convex lenses bend light inward, bringing rays together at a focal point.

options.text: Diverges (spreads out) the light rays
options.feedback: Spreading light out is what a concave lens does, not a convex one.

options.text: Completely blocks all light
options.feedback: A lens transmits and bends light, it doesn't block it entirely.

options.text: Reflects all light back the way it came
options.feedback: Lenses refract (bend) light as it passes through, rather than reflecting it back.

hard.text: Which type of lens is typically used to correct nearsightedness (difficulty seeing distant objects)?

options.text: Concave lens
options.feedback: Correct -- concave lenses diverge light before it enters the eye, correcting how nearsighted eyes over-focus light.

options.text: Convex lens
options.feedback: Convex lenses are generally used to correct farsightedness, not nearsightedness.

options.text: A flat piece of glass
options.feedback: Flat glass doesn't bend light in a way that corrects vision problems.

options.text: No lens is needed for this condition
options.feedback: Nearsightedness is a real, correctable vision condition that specifically benefits from a particular lens shape.

easy.hard: This lens bulges outward, with its greatest thickness right at its center.
easy.medium: This lens is fatter in the center than around its edges.
easy.easy: This lens is fatter in the middle than at its edges.

medium.hard: This lens shape bends parallel light rays inward so they meet at a single focal point.
medium.medium: This type of lens bends light rays inward to meet at a point.
medium.easy: This lens bends light rays together to a single point.

hard.hard: This lens shape spreads incoming light rays apart before they reach the eye, compensating for an eye that focuses images too early.
hard.medium: This lens spreads light out slightly before it enters the eye, which helps with seeing distant objects clearly.
hard.easy: This lens spreads light out a bit, which helps someone see far-away things more clearly.
